title: Verité Research drives global debt agenda at IMF–WB Annual Meetings  | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 04:54
-     - 6

Verité Research yesterday said it played a notable role at the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (WB) Group in Bangkok, driving strategic dialogues on debt, inequality, and governance through policy roundtables, high-level investor briefings, and multilateral stakeholder engagements. 

The Verité Research delegation to the Annual Meetings, held from 12 to 18 October, included Executive Director Dr. Nishan de Mel, Corporate Director – Strategic Planning Inoshini Perera, and Lead Economist Raj Prabu Rajakulendran. 

During the Meetings, the think tank convened two roundtables, co-sponsored two Civil Society Policy Forum (CSPF) sessions, served on expert panels in closed-door discussions, and met with IMF, Government, donor, and civil society counterparts. The delegation also conducted technical briefings for international sovereign debt investors on Sri Lanka’s economic outlook and IMF program implementation. 

The first side-event roundtable examined how Governance-Linked Bonds, a novel sovereign debt instrument designed by Verité Research for Sri Lanka as a world first, could be applied to other debt-vulnerable nations. The second roundtable explored structural safeguards to protect democratic governance within IMF programs, addressing concerns that reform frameworks can inadvertently bypass parliaments, judiciary bodies, and independent national institutions. 

As part of the CSPF, the civil society track of the official IMF–World Bank program, Verité Research co-sponsored sessions focusing on fiscal transparency and accountability across the Asia-Pacific region, alongside multilateral responses to nations facing severe debt burdens. 

Additionally, the delegation participated in closed-door roundtables with international debt managers, legal experts, and development partners to address hidden fiscal risks operating outside headline public debt statistics. The team also contributed to a panel on policy advocacy in Asia at a partner foundation’s forum, and provided media commentary on Sri Lanka’s fiscal accountability structures.

title: BRISL to host seminar for undergraduates on Belt and Road Initiative in Colombo today | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 04:52
-     - 4

Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka (BRISL) will today (19) kick off a two-day undergraduate seminar titled “Sri Lanka and the Belt and Road Initiative: Building Synergies for Sustainable Development” at Amari Colombo.

It will bring together 25 undergraduate students from the University of Colombo, University of Sri Jayewardenepura, and University of Kelaniya, representing the disciplines of Economics, Business Economics, International Relations, and International Studies.

The initiative aims to deepen students’ understanding of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), its implications for Sri Lanka’s economic development, and emerging opportunities in trade, investment, infrastructure, connectivity, and international cooperation.

The two-day program will feature discussions led by distinguished academics, diplomats, and development experts, including Prof. Sirimal Abeyratne, Dr. George I.H. Cooke, Admiral (Prof.) Jayanath Colombage, Dr. Palitha T.B. Kohona, and Dr. Vagisha Gunasekara.

BRISL Director Maya Majueran will deliver a presentation titled “High-Quality BRI and Sri Lanka: Unlocking New Pathways for Sustainable Development.”

The sessions will explore the historical and diplomatic dimensions of the BRI, Sri Lanka’s strategic autonomy in the Indian Ocean, development financing, debt restructuring, economic opportunities, and human resource development.

A key feature of the seminar will be educational visits to Huawei Technologies Lanka, Port City Colombo, and Colombo International Container Terminals (CICT), offering participants first-hand exposure to digital technologies, major infrastructure investments, port operations, and Sri Lanka’s evolving role as a regional trade and logistics hub.

The program is designed to bridge academic learning with practical experience while encouraging informed discussion of both the opportunities and challenges associated with the BRI.

Participants will be nominated by their respective universities based on academic merit, ensuring meaningful engagement among undergraduate students.

The seminar will conclude with a certificate presentation and closing dinner tomorrow (20), attended by representatives of the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in Sri Lanka.

Through this initiative, BRISL seeks to strengthen academic engagement, encourage knowledge sharing, and provide young Sri Lankans with greater exposure to international economic cooperation and sustainable development opportunities.

title: Entrepreneurs share lessons in resilience and leadership at AAT Sri Lanka Conference 2026 | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 04:49
-     - 2

From left: Vito Pizza Group Managing Director Ranil Goonatilleke, Jack Fruit Ceylon Managing Director Dulanjana Vithanage, Wild Cookbook culinary content creator Charith N. Silva, Castoranets Singapore Vice President of Finance and Administration Bhagya Senevirathne and AAT Sri Lanka President by Dr. Chamara Bandara

Businesses are rarely built according to plan. Sometimes the turning point is a crisis, a failed experiment, a lost job or simply the decision to take a calculated risk.

That reality came through in very different ways as entrepreneurs and corporate leaders shared their personal journeys at the closing leadership panel of the AAT Sri Lanka Conference 2026, offering lessons in discipline, resilience, adaptability and ownership.

The session, Transformative Leadership: Lead to Inspire, was moderated AAT Sri Lanka President by Dr. Chamara Bandara and held on the final day of the conference, themed Precision of Power, at Waters Edge, Battaramulla, on 8 and 9 September.

The panel featured chef and Wild Cookbook culinary content creator Charith N. Silva, Jack Fruit Ceylon Managing Director Dulanjana Vithanage, Vito Pizza Group Managing Director Ranil Goonatilleke, and Castoranets Singapore Vice President of Finance and Administration Bhagya Senevirathne. A recorded address by Araliya Group of Companies Chairman Dudley Sirisena was also screened after he was unable to attend in person.

Entrepreneurship beyond necessity

Opening the session, Dr. Bandara said his own entrepreneurial outlook had been shaped early in his career after questioning why so many graduates sought jobs rather than creating them.

He noted that developing countries recorded higher rates of entrepreneurship than developed ones, although this was largely driven by necessity rather than scalable market opportunity.

“In developing countries, entrepreneurship is mostly driven by necessity and unemployment,” he said, citing Sirisena’s rise from a small village rice business to a large corporate enterprise as an example of scaling beyond necessity-driven beginnings.

Discipline as the foundation of leadership

In his recorded address, Sirisena said leading a disciplined personal life was the most fundamental requirement for becoming a leader in business or society.

“Before becoming a social leader, the most appropriate way to gain experience is to become a leader to yourself,” he said, recalling that he had grown up without discipline but corrected his path through life experience and guidance.

Sirisena said accounting and commerce education formed a core foundation for structured business planning, while a disciplined lifestyle could help entrepreneurs overcome early capital constraints by building trust with family, friends and financial institutions.

He recalled washing dishes at wealthier friends’ functions during his early years to remain close to networks that could help him access capital.

He also warned against dishonesty in business. “Dishonesty destroys all growth and eventually reduces a person to the lowest social tier, regardless of their education level,” he said.

When crisis forces a business to change

For Ranil Goonatilleke, crisis became the catalyst for changing the direction of his business.

He said Vito Pizza began almost by accident, evolving from wood-fired pizza served to foreign guests at his family’s hotel in Kandy. The Easter Sunday attacks and later COVID-19 brought foreign arrivals to a halt, forcing the business to reconsider its market.

“We asked ourselves, ‘What do we do now? Who do we cater to?’” he said.

The company launched a delivery service within three days of the lockdown, at one point delivering pizza from Kandy to Galagedara.

Goonatilleke credited his accounting background, gained while working at two hotels in Kandy, with giving him the financial literacy and banking exposure needed to later secure funding for his first property.

“Accountants handle bank loans and documentation for chairmen every day, so why can’t we do it for ourselves?” he said.

The business has since expanded to Colombo, Peradeniya, Galle and Negombo.

Turning an unwanted crop into an export business

Dulanjana Vithanage’s journey with Jack Fruit Ceylon began far from any early entrepreneurial ambition.

Growing up in a remote village in Galle, he recalled fallen jackfruit routinely obstructing footpaths. “As a child, the tree I hated most was the jackfruit tree,” he said.

After abandoning early ambitions in medicine and law, he pursued Commerce. An experience observing a hospital finance manager directing the work of doctors and engineers later shaped his interest in management.

Vithanage described mobilising university students across faculties to survey why communities avoided eating jackfruit and eventually developing high-protein jackfruit-based noodles and pasta with support from a small government grant and self-funded machinery.

“We built machinery, failed at candy making, and once dimmed the entire village’s lights when turning on our machine,” he said.

The business has since grown into an ISO-standard factory employing 30 people and supported by 406 rural suppliers, with exports reaching international markets.

From hospitality to 20 million followers

Charith N. Silva, who spent seven years in the hotel industry before pursuing content creation full-time, said he began publishing short-form culinary videos in 2019 after losing his hospitality job to the pandemic.

He later resigned from full-time employment after recovering from COVID-19 to pursue the venture entirely.

“You must have a Plan B when taking risks,” he said, adding that managing younger staff required leaders to set aside ego.

Silva said his content now reaches more than 20 million followers globally, a following that came with a responsibility not to influence audiences negatively.

Creating ownership within organisations

Bhagya Senevirathne, who lost the use of both legs and her right hand in an accident at age 16, said she completed her Ordinary Level examinations the same year and later graduated with first-class honours from Rajarata University, despite employers initially doubting her physical capacity for certain roles.

She joined MAS Holdings as an intern and later led a SAP system implementation and supported data migration during pandemic lockdowns, before leaving after fourteen years to start her own venture.

Senevirathne described intrapreneurship as treating one’s workplace as a second home and taking full ownership of organisational growth.

“Education is the foundation, but experience shapes our journey. Not everyone can be a founding entrepreneur, but we can work alongside one and add value,” she said.

“Since people spend much of their lives at work, entrepreneurs must create a sense of belonging. Even after starting my own business, I still feel that MAS is mine because its culture gave me that feeling.”

Leadership that inspires action

Summarising the session, Vithanage said education remained a full foundation for both entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs, while Silva said a business depended entirely on its staff and required treating them with respect.

Senevirathne said creating a workplace where employees felt ownership was central to sustained success.

Closing the panel, Dr. Bandara urged attendees to apply the lessons shared.

“When you act as a leader, you inspire followers. Transform yourself and transform those around you,” he said.

title: Ajantha Dharmasiri’s Management Musings: Building bridge from reality to results | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 03:28
-     - 18

Dharmasiri correctly concludes that modern society must learn to screen its digital information flows with intense care. It is our collective responsibility to actively accept what is beneficial and systematically reject what is harmful. A digital foe can be converted into an educational friend, but that transformation depends entirely on our own media literacy and discipline

Ajantha Dharmasiri, a senior professor at the Postgraduate Institute of Management (PIM) and a regular columnist for the Daily FT, has released his newest book titled Management Musings. It contains 30 newspaper articles he had penned from 2021 to 2023 on numerous management issues. This is his 17th publication overall. Dharmasiri has long been an active writer, public lecturer, and human resource expert. Having served as the Director of PIM for two consecutive terms and as the former President of the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management (CIPM) Sri Lanka, he is also a much-loved teacher by his students. This new publication successfully collects some of his most impactful public writings in print form, ensuring they are accessible to a wider readership in Sri Lanka and abroad.

The book offers a direct path toward addressing modern workplace challenges by moving beyond simple common sense into the realm of structured corporate achievements. Through his columns, Dharmasiri functions as a critical link between complex academic theories and the daily ground realities faced by practicing business managers. By compiling these pieces, he provides leaders with a practical handbook that translates everyday corporate situations into sustainable organisational results.

Deeply personal anchor: Family and mentorship

Dharmasiri has always been a dedicated family man who has remained deeply connected to his household throughout his professional career. The present book is intimately dedicated to his family members: his wife, his daughter, and his late son, who left him before attaining adulthood. This connection to family is by no means limited to those in the immediate domestic circle. Within the detailed acknowledgements of the book, he explicitly gives credit to his brothers, parents, and in-laws for shaping his character and making him the individual he is today. He reserves a profound amount of gratitude and particular credit for his late son, whose memory heavily influences his worldview.

In one of his specific articles, Dharmasiri names two distinct mentors who shaped his life path. The first is the late Prof. Uditha Liyanage, a highly respected ex-Director of PIM who directly supervised his doctoral research work. Professor Liyanage served as his traditional academic mentor, providing intellectual guidance, rigorous research standards, and professional direction. However, in the same breath, Dharmasiri gives immense credit to his late son for serving as a "reverse mentor"—a concept where the younger generation guides the older generation.

While reverse mentoring might seem like a strange type of relationship to traditionalists, it is increasingly common and highly necessary in our modern world, as Dharmasiri explains. Belonging to Generation X, he found himself being continuously guided by his son, who belonged to Generation Z. In all matters concerning rapid developments in Information and Communication Technology (ICT), digital media, and modern computing trends, it was his son who proudly served as his Guru.

This dynamic extended far beyond mere technical assistance. Says Dharmasiri: "I learnt how to be cheerful from him. He was always with a smile. This was repeatedly mentioned by his friends who came to pay their last respect. When I was stressful and tired, his warmth and cheerfulness was a relief for me."

Therefore, his son was not merely a technology guide, but a highly effective stress-beater during times of intense professional pressure. This candid admission of what he learned from his young child illuminates the deeply personal, vulnerable side of an otherwise authoritative academic figure. Yet, for many parents who raise children belonging to the new digital generation, this experience is entirely relatable. In a similar personal parallel, it was my own son who first introduced me to contemporary authors like Dan Brown, Michael Crichton, and Bill Bryson, proving that knowledge flow between generations is truly a two-way street.

Dharmasiri has demonstrated his humility and humbleness by admitting that he was a product of two mentors. On the academic side, it was the late Prof. Uditha Liyanage who fashioned him to a world class teacher and researcher. On the technical and personal side, his late son had guided him through the technological developments of the day and provided him with a powerful tool to address the challenges posed by a highly stressful world.

Power of alliteration: Making complex systems memorable

A defining trait of Dharmasiri’s teaching career is his special skill in breaking down incredibly complex institutional systems into easily graspable terms. He does this by organising his frameworks using words that begin with the exact same letter of the alphabet. His postgraduate students have long noted that this systematic technique helps them visualise and remember the entire big picture involved in an otherwise overwhelming corporate framework. Ordinary readers will easily appreciate this stylistic tool, as it removes the dry, dense nature of typical business textbooks.

In the prologue to the book, he explains that his musings are designed to help a reader execute a four-step mental cycle: recognise, relate, reflect, and reinforce. First, a manager must recognise the unique personal features of diverse people in the workplace. Next, they must relate these basic concepts directly to the current operational challenges faced by their specific company. Following this, they are urged to reflect deeply on the core human struggles of managing performance, before finally reinforcing positive, professional behaviors across multiple operational fronts.

When addressing individuals who wish to pursue higher education, he presents another memorable alphabetical structure. He notes that a master's degree aspirant should strictly evaluate a business school based on seven key vectors: reputation, reliability, relevance, rigour, reach, response, and research. By analysing these criteria, an applicant ensures they are not just buying a credential but are training themselves to put Mind Before Action—offering a completely fresh, strategic meaning for the traditional MBA abbreviation.

This deliberate method is also visible when he addresses the topic of people management. An employer who genuinely wishes to look after their staff must concentrate on nine distinct operational behaviors, all beginning with the letter C:

1.‘Connecting’ authentically with the team on a regular basis.

2.Prioritising long-term ‘career’ development opportunities.

3.Establishing absolute ‘clarity’ of instructions to prevent workplace anxiety.

4.‘Conveying’ the clear message regarding institutional values and goals.

5.Consistently ‘congratulating’ on good work to maintain moral momentum.

6.Ensuring visible ‘contribution’ recognition so individual efforts are validated.

7.‘Controlling’ for consistency and conformance to keep operational quality stable.

8.Preserving the ‘credibility’ of the work standards across all departments.

9.Active ‘confidence’ inculcation in the employee to empower decentralised decision-making.

These structured frameworks serve as highly practical tools. Any manager wishing to improve their day-to-day operations can easily write these simple alliterative points on short notes and hang them around their bedroom mirror or office workstation as a constant mental reminder.

Through the steady publication of these collected essays, Dharmasiri succeeds in merging messy day-to-day corporate realities with clear business results. In the epilogue of the book, he introduces a timeless philosophical perspective by quoting the famous 19th-century French writer Alexandre Dumas, who famously observed that "All human wisdom is contained in these two words, wait and hope

Navigating the modern infodemic: Friend or foe?

During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, the entire global population faced an identical problem: how could individuals at the micro level, nations at the macro level, and the international community at the global level successfully overcome a sudden catastrophe? While medical professionals worked on treatments, social media channels were deployed across the globe. Unfortunately, these networks were used both correctly to spread vital safety data and incorrectly to spread panic.

Dharmasiri highlights this modern crisis by utilising a specific term coined by the World Health Organisation (WHO): the oncoming surge of digital misinformation known as an 'Infodemic'. In his writing, he poses a fundamental question for our modern age: is this digital information explosion a friend or a foe?

He carefully breaks down the two sides of the issue. Accurate, timely information during a public health crisis acts as a vital friend, providing clear instructions that save lives, coordinate medical distribution, and lower public anxiety. Conversely, bad information, unverified rumors, and malicious conspiracy theories act as a dangerous foe, causing widespread public confusion, institutional distrust, and harmful risk-taking behaviour.

Dharmasiri correctly concludes that modern society must learn to screen its digital information flows with intense care. It is our collective responsibility to actively accept what is beneficial and systematically reject what is harmful. A digital foe can be converted into an educational friend, but that transformation depends entirely on our own media literacy and discipline.

This management lesson applies far beyond the historical boundaries of a global pandemic. In our everyday lives, we are continuously bombarded by false, altered, or highly exaggerated misinformation every single second. These notes are frequently pushed by interested parties, political actors, or commercial entities seeking to exploit our attention and guide us down the wrong path. Dharmasiri reminds us that it is our absolute personal duty to defend our minds from these well-orchestrated digital attacks.

Analysis of a popular teledrama in management perspective

A striking musing he has presented in his collection is the analysis of a popular Sinhala teledrama, Nadagamkarayo or Traditional Drama Folks, telecast for over one year. Management or economics is not a subject that is learned only through textbooks. Since both deal with human beings, they are related to the contemporary cultural and societal ethos. Any effective sustained learning should draw on examples from the critical evaluation of that ethos as presented in contemporary artwork. Dharmasiri has used this universal truth to teach us what management lessons could be learned from this particular drama. Obviously, he has singled out this drama due to its immense popularity among Sri Lankan TV viewers. 

In the story, there is a young entrepreneur who had started his life as an illicit bootlegger. However, he changes himself through wise counsel of elders in the village. However, the Government officials who should support new businesses in the village have a totally apathetic approach to them. Says Dharmasiri: ‘The questionable support by the so-called Government officials towards the SMEs is realistically portrayed here. Among many inefficient and insensitive State officials, there was one Business Development Officer who went out of the way to help the four youngsters in going for a business registration, obtaining a bank loan, and purchasing of machinery and equipment. Ironically, she is harassed by another colleague who accused her of doing more to get a promotion’. To succeed in their new venture, they do a SWOT analysis, carefully analysing the Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats to them on the advice of the Chief Incumbent of the Buddhist temple in the village.

This is where the management perspective comes to the picture. 

This is the crude reality which Sri Lanka faces today. SME sector which accounts for about 50-60% of national wealth creation and an equal number of employment generation is given step-motherly treatment by the Government officials who are there to promote the same. That is one of the reasons for Sri Lanka to getting trapped in in eternal circle of poverty and economic stagnation. Dharmasiri has beautifully presented this stark truth which may not be palatable to those to whom it matters.

Management musings offered to you an assortment of serene sharing towards meaningfully engaging the precious human resources with care and clarity. It is a matter of envisioning the future and endeavouring to make it a reality. The twin challenge of employee wellbeing and enterprise progress can be balanced by ensuring humane results. With clarity of purpose and commitment in action we should strive for excellence as essence

Merging reality with results: A guide for modern leaders

Through the steady publication of these collected essays, Dharmasiri succeeds in merging messy day-to-day corporate realities with clear business results. In the epilogue of the book, he introduces a timeless philosophical perspective by quoting the famous 19th-century French writer Alexandre Dumas, who famously observed that "All human wisdom is contained in these two words, wait and hope."

This observation serves as a vital lesson for contemporary corporate executives who often operate under the pressure of immediate deadlines. The management guru advises leaders that they must not simply jump to instant conclusions when an unexpected crisis emerges. Instead, a wise leader waits patiently until the smoke created by an explosive corporate situation completely dissipates, allowing them to view the entire picture with an objective mind.

In the epilogue, Dharmasiri beautifully summarises the core purpose of his essays, offering a long-term vision for the future of professional leadership:

He says: "Management musings offered to you an assortment of serene sharing towards meaningfully engaging the precious human resources with care and clarity. It is a matter of envisioning the future and endeavouring to make it a reality. The twin challenge of employee wellbeing and enterprise progress can be balanced by ensuring humane results. With clarity of purpose and commitment in action we should strive for excellence as essence."

This final perspective encapsulates the lifelong teaching philosophy of a scholar who has trained thousands of business students. By focusing heavily on the human element, ensuring absolute clarity of purpose, and practicing patience during chaotic times, Management Musings provides an enduring blueprint for any leader striving to bridge the gap between initial corporate reality and ultimate organisational results.

(The writer, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, can be reached at waw1949@gmail.com)

title: Countrywide power failure:  A national security wake-up call | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 03:21
-     - 12

The cascading collapse of Sri Lanka’s national electricity grid on Saturday, 17 October 2026, was more than a technical failure. For several hours the island was without grid power after instability in the transmission network around midday. The National System Operator began restoration using available hydro resources, with partial supplies returning to several districts by afternoon and fuller recovery targeted for the evening. Rooftop solar owners were asked to disconnect, and major water treatment plants temporarily halted operations.

From a national security standpoint, electricity is foundational infrastructure. When it fails at scale, the effects reach command and control, hospitals, water supply, communications, transport nodes, financial platforms, and the operational readiness of security agencies. Even a relatively short outage reveals the margin that separates normal functioning from systemic strain. The fact that a demonstrated vulnerability could again place the entire country in darkness within a short interval raises a further question: whether the risk was adequately visualised and treated as a standing contingency after the comparable failure of February 2025.

What the event revealed

The precise trigger remains under investigation. Early indications point to system instability, possibly compounded by a preceding technical issue at a Kotmale facility and by the “Sunny Saturday” dynamic, high rooftop solar output on a bright day coinciding with lower weekend demand. Sri Lanka’s installed solar capacity now exceeds 3,000 MW against typical daytime demand of 2,000–2,500 MW. When non-synchronous generation forms a large share of supply, conventional synchronous plants that provide system inertia are often minimised. A modest disturbance can then produce voltage or frequency deviations, large-scale inverter disconnections, and a cascade that outruns under-frequency load shedding and other controls.

This mechanism is not new. On 9 February 2025 a similar islandwide blackout followed a minor substation fault while solar supplied more than half of demand. Expert analysis attributed the scale of the collapse to low system inertia. Recommendations that followed included updated inverter settings, selective curtailment, and plans for battery storage and pumped hydro. Some steps were taken. Yet the recurrence within twenty months shows that the deeper lesson, high penetration of inverter-based generation without matching grid strength and controllable resources creates a system prone to rapid cascade, was not closed with sufficient speed or institutional force. My

The intelligence and security dimension

Intelligence agencies are not grid operators. They do not manage frequency control, inertia, or solar curtailment; those remain the responsibilities of the National System Operator, the energy ministry, and the regulator. Their proper role is to identify vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure that could be exploited, to provide early warning of deliberate threats (cyber intrusion into control systems, physical sabotage, or hybrid operations timed with technical failure), and to contribute to whole-of-government risk assessments that treat cascading infrastructure collapse as a national security contingency.

If the demonstrated risk of a rapid, island-wide blackout under high-solar, low-inertia conditions was not adequately captured, escalated, and followed through after February 2025, that constitutes a gap. The shortfall is more likely one of default than design: sectoral silos in which energy planners focus on generation targets while security structures focus on kinetic or foreign threats; critical-infrastructure protection that remains underdeveloped as a standing function; and lessons that are documented but lose urgency once power is restored. Joint exercising between system operators, intelligence, disaster management, defence, health, and water authorities appears limited. Once a vulnerability has been shown to be capable of darkening the country at once, failure to close it within a reasonable interval becomes a governance and security issue, not merely a technical delay.

Were we ready?

Planning frameworks exist. Institutional disaster management plans cover the electricity sector. Under-frequency load shedding, black-start procedures, and protective systems are in place. System controllers have previously averted full collapses on comparable days, and battery storage and longer-term pumped-storage projects are advancing. These are real assets. Readiness, however, is measured by outcomes. The second major cascading failure in less than two years indicates that contingency arrangements have not kept pace with the generation mix. Distributed solar remains only partially visible and controllable in real time. Critical facilities continue to rely heavily on local diesel generators whose fuel logistics and endurance have not been systematically stress-tested. The temporary halt at major water plants illustrated the tight interdependency of utilities and the narrow surplus available for public-health continuity. Clear, pre-agreed decision authorities and practiced multi-agency protocols for a prolonged outage are not publicly evident. In short, technical tools exist, but the broader contingency architecture required to prevent or rapidly contain a national cascade remains incomplete.

Economic and perceptual consequences

The direct costs of a multi-hour islandwide outage include unserved energy, temporary business interruption, generator fuel, and secondary effects on water supply and logistics. Earlier events of this nature have been estimated to cost several billion rupees once both utility losses and wider productivity impacts are counted. A Saturday outage reduces the absolute figure relative to a weekday, yet the cumulative damage from recurring reliability problems is larger. Sri Lanka is still consolidating recovery from the 2022 crisis. Investors in manufacturing, information technology, business-process outsourcing, and tourism treat infrastructure reliability as a basic condition. Repeated failures raise operating costs, complicate financing, and can slow the return of higher-value activity.

International coverage of the October outage has so far been largely factual, noting the grid trip, the possible contribution of excess solar, and the earlier 2025 incident. Recurrence itself, however, enters the record. Neighbouring countries and external partners assess state capacity partly through the performance of basic infrastructure. A pattern of cascading failures linked to unmanaged renewable growth, without commensurate investment in storage and grid flexibility, can reinforce perceptions of institutional lag and influence investment and financing decisions.

Closing the gap

The appropriate response is not to reverse the energy transition. Renewables reduce fuel-import dependence and carry strategic value. The requirement is to match the speed of capacity addition with the physical and institutional capacity to operate the system securely, and to treat the residual risk as a standing national contingency.

Priority steps include faster deployment of grid-scale battery storage and other resources that restore inertia and provide fast frequency response; enforceable technical standards for inverters together with better real-time visibility and control of distributed generation; strengthened black-start and selective islanding capabilities for hospitals, security nodes, water plants, and key communications; and regularly exercised whole-of-government plans that integrate the system operator with intelligence, defence, police, disaster management, health, and water authorities. An independent technical review of the 17 October event, comparable to the process that followed February 2025, would identify remaining gaps and create accountability for implementation. Intelligence and security structures should maintain an updated assessment of critical-infrastructure cascade risks so that known vulnerabilities do not remain unaddressed between incidents.

Conclusion

The islandwide power failure of 17 October 2026 was contained in time and is being restored. It nevertheless reconfirmed a structural vulnerability in infrastructure that underpins national functioning. The interval between a demonstrated technical warning and effective systemic remedy is itself a security gap. In a system where high solar penetration can, under certain conditions, place the country in darkness at once, resilience requires continuous investment, joint exercising, and the willingness to close known risks before the next sunny low-demand day.

Sri Lanka has shown the operational ability to begin recovery promptly. The larger test is whether the lessons of 2025 and 2026 produce durable improvements in grid strength, contingency depth, and inter-agency readiness, including the intelligence community’s contribution to visualising and elevating critical-infrastructure risks. Electricity reliability is not solely an economic or engineering matter. It is a standing component of national security. Treating it as such will better serve both the daily needs of citizens and the longer-term stability of the state.

(This analysis is offered in the interest of national security, institutional reform, and public safety)

(The author is a retired Senior Superintendent of Police, former Head of the Counter-Terrorism Desk at the State Intelligence Service, and the author of ‘Security Beyond Enforcement: Practical Approaches for a Safer Nation (2026).’ He can be reached at mahildole54@gmail.com)

title: The balance of power | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 03:15
-     - 11

The valiant

Centuries ago, the intervention of a Persian king, restored a degree of balance of power in the West Asian region. In the 6thc, BCE, Cyrus the Great of Persia, put a stop to the aggressive expansionism of the Babylonian empire and set the exiled Jews free.  

After Cyrus’s death, his successor Darius was made aware of his predecessors’ plans to do even more. Commissioning some competent Jews, he fulfilled Cyrus’s intentions by restoring the ravaged city of Jerusalem and its venerated temple. 

The Jews were overwhelmed. They would remember the valiant one who revived the essence of their nationhood. And so, the story of Cyrus the Persian, acknowledged as the ‘Anointed Deliverer’, the ‘Messiah’, came to be etched in the Jewish Scriptures (The Bible-Ezra 1- 6:15, Isaiah 44: 28, 45: 1-13).

Empire and empires

This stirring story impacted Christianity as well. As former Jews, the earliest Christians were familiar with the hardship experienced under Babylonian imperialism. This led to the secret identification of the then brutal Roman Empire, as ‘Babylon’. The pseudonym worked so well that some Christian writings and communities applied it to other marauding forces that crushed peoples and looted their lands.

Vain politics

Today the world witnesses an ironic alliance of relentless bullying between the progeny of ‘Babylon’ and Jew. Together the US and Israel do to others what Babylon did to the Jews, and what their Book tells the Jews they are never to do to others.    

The alliance’s agenda is straightforward. While one randomly ridicules and threatens sovereign nations, the other is quick to fabricate evidence that leads to the decimation of infants, children and unarmed civilians; all on the pretext of self-defence.  Thereafter, security zones carved out on other people’s property mock what is left of International law, ‘friendly’ nations are intimidated into buying killing devices at thumping profits and military bases emerge on these territories in exchange for protection. The war with Iran, Cyrus’ Persia of today, is integral to this agenda.

Enter the villain

Iran, one of the most ancient and advanced civilisations of the world, has since its Islamic revolution of 1979 come under a despotic theocratic governance. It has crushed internal dissent and the clamour for participatory governance among its own people, prevented the growth of democratic institutions, trained and financed para-military forces to resist Israel’s settler colonialism and challenged the influx of western interests in the region. In return Iran has been relentlessly caricatured as global villain and subject to the wrath of the western mind- set and its propaganda industry.

The campaign to demonise Iran has been so clever that many of her neighbours who share a long cultural history, stand shoulder to shoulder today with vain intruders bent on crushing the only nation it cannot subdue, in a region they have no business to meddle in.

The nerve to be

Wars do strange things. They slaughter good men and women on all sides, cause chaos and misery wherever it spreads and never stop to explain to the children who survive, that this madness was simply to satisfy the egos of the vain.   

But wars also change human perception. And there are signs that the current war on Iran, (It must never be the ‘Iranian war’, as it should never have been the ‘Korean war’, the ‘Vietnam war’, the ‘Afghanistan war’ and so on), is changing global perception.

Slowly, the devious stereotype of global saviours versus regional villains, is being redefined. While the hard questions on participatory, good governance must remain to haunt and transform Iran, the villain is now being acknowledged, however grudgingly, as the one nation that refused to back down in the face of global bullying. This too at tremendous personal cost to the lives of its people, infra-structure and future stability. In a world of cowardly political expediency, costly resistance attracts attention; even admiration.       

There is more. The resilience of the vilified villain in the current war appears to have strengthened the nerve of the repeatedly humiliated European and British allies of the alliance, who at last learnt to say ‘no’. A first, to an ‘order’ to join an unprovoked and senseless far away war, backed with a second, when pressed to police the Straits of Hormuz. Typical of handling the playground bully, all it takes is for one little girl to hold her ground.  

It does not stop here. Sheer desperation at Iran’s unsettling tenacity shamelessly drove Babylon into the arms of other neutral powers that it repeatedly ridicules and badgers with threats of tariffs and more tariffs.  Regardless of a sudden demonstration of charming diplomacy, these nations would have no part in twisting Iran’s arm. Some instead, seized the opportunity to address Babylon on its arbitrary violation of International Law and warned it to refrain from global bullying.  Since then, there have been less threats on the annexation of Greenland and interference in Cuba’s internal affairs.

The right balance

Like war does, resistance to war also does strange things. While the refusal to yield stimulates active defiance among some, and strongly worded objections from others, the outcome of the current conflict is hugely unpredictable. An independent, safe and stable region, made up of independent, safe and stable nations, is many, many courageous interventions and many, many wise negotiations away.  

But one thing is clear. Isolated from its traditional allies, subject to straight talk from neutral nations and under growing pressure from saner elements at home, the vain find themselves uncomfortably seated as equals at one table. Here, Iranian geo-political strategies coupled with a measured readiness to return to arms in the event that table agreements are violated, will hold them; but for a while.      

Given this footpath to a balance of power that Cyrus’s Persia of today has paved, it is now left to all who value the sovereignty and dignity of all nations, theirs included, and the indispensability of International law, to step out and help steer this momentum.

In the event that this happens, dismantling the visible acts of global bullying alone, will not be enough. The impulse of this crime, flourishing brazenly in the big businesses and assembly halls in the big cities of the world, and more subtly tucked away in the fabric of reputed places of learning, religiosity and leisure, will also have to be called out and neutralised.

Postscript 

At the time of writing, a humanitarian crisis looms over Lanka’s southern seas. Historically renowned for her spontaneous hospitality  even in the worst of times, Lanka finds herself constrained from responding to the desperate cries for supplies; water, food and fuel, from a stranded fleet of commercial ships, simply because they fly the Iranian flag. Regrettably, Babylon’s typical threat of sanctions appears to be driving our economically vulnerable Island nation to the brink of compromising our time tested right to be humane.             

With peace and blessings to all.

title: Sri Lanka’s terror law could cost it a trade lifeline | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 01:46
-     - 4

JAAF does not argue that Sri Lanka should have no counter-terrorism law. Its case is simpler: a law this broad, with so little judicial oversight, puts at risk the trade access that supports hundreds of thousands of livelihoods

By Joint Apparel Association Forum

Sri Lanka has spent four decades trying to rid itself of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), a law used so freely that even its authors, in the 1979 parliament, called it temporary. The Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA), gazetted and tabled last week, is meant to replace it. Critics say it keeps much of the old machinery. That matters beyond the human-rights lobby, because the EU's GSP+ trade concession depends on it.

The price of access

GSP+ is not a gift. It gives Sri Lankan goods duty-free entry to the EU in exchange for compliance with 27 international conventions on human rights, labour and the environment, a list that grows to 32 in 2027-28. The UN and the EU have said for years that any PTA replacement must meet those standards: narrow definitions, protection for association, assembly and expression, andWhat is wrong with the Bill

courts that can check the Executive.

A cushion under a weak sector

Apparel is the country's biggest export, worth about $ 5 billion a year and over 40% of merchandise exports. Fabric and textiles add roughly 

$ 522 million. The EU takes a little over 30% of the total; in the first half of the year Sri Lanka exported $ 705 million of apparel to the EU.

The sector can ill afford a shock. In the first half of 2026, Sri Lanka’s apparel exports to the EU fell 8% compared to 2025. By contrast the EU’s import of apparel from China grew 5% whilst Vietnam grew 9%. The writing is on the wall; Sri Lanka is losing valuable market share to Europe whilst other countries grow. Europe is a market Sri Lanka can least afford to weaken.

What is wrong with the Bill

Legal experts who have followed four attempts at PTA reform since 2018 say the text improves on earlier drafts but still falls short. Their main complaints:

Where are the judges?

The common thread is the absence of judicial oversight. Nobody doubts that a State needs security powers. The question is who checks them. Ordinary law keeps a magistrate in the loop, and stakeholders have asked why this Bill does not.

The fixes are modest. Let magistrates weigh evidence before approving detention, give courts a role in proscription, and leave arrests to the Police. 

The Bill had its first reading on 6 October. Under the Constitution, petitions to the Supreme Court can be filed within 14 days of a Bill reaching Parliament's order paper, and the Court then has three weeks to rule. A debate is therefore unlikely before November. Campaigners say the Government wants the Bill passed before the Budget, which is presented on 12 November. The Court can rule on constitutionality but not on policy, so committee-stage amendments are the realistic route to change. The Government accepted several suggestions on last November's draft, which suggests it can still be moved.

The industry's case

JAAF does not argue that Sri Lanka should have no counter-terrorism law. Its case is simpler: a law this broad, with so little judicial oversight, puts at risk the trade access that supports hundreds of thousands of livelihoods. The current cycle of the GSP+ ends in 2027, and Sri Lanka, like any other beneficiary country needs to reapply for the new cycle of the scheme. The PSTA, in its current format, is very likely to be a roadblock in country’s application for the new cycle. The EU is a bureaucracy, and if Sri Lanka’s application for the new round of GSP+ is unsuccessful because of the PSTA, this will leave the country without its largest trade preference program. Fixing the Bill now is cheap. Fixing it afterwards will not be.

title: Prevention of Organised Crime Bill: Flooding the zone? | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 01:45
-     - 10

This law is being enacted as part of a flood-the-zone strategy without any public or stakeholder consultation not because new offences are needed, but because the security establishment and the Government want a workaround for the safeguards in existing law. The flood is not entirely of disconnected, discrete pieces of legislation. In this case, part of it is the organically connected PSTA and POCA

It appears that some in our Government have become acolytes of Steve Bannon, President Trump’s Rasputin. Bannon famously said: "The real opposition is the media. And the way to deal with them is to flood the zone with shit.” The idea is to overwhelm your critics (not limited to media in the Sri Lankan context) with multiple initiatives at the same time so that they are compelled to let some pass.

First, it was the 22nd Amendment. Then it was the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA). The NGO (Registration and Supervision) Bill, and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (POCA), Prevention of Foreign Terrorist Fighters, amendments to the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance . . . they keep coming. Who has the time and the resources to analyse all these? Who can mount efforts to reduce the dangers posed to human liberty by this flood through challenges before the Supreme Court in the permitted two weeks, or by other means?

The flood is real, but there may be more to it.

Whack-a-mole

The Government’s tactics also evoke the arcade game of whack-a-mole. As the player whacks down one mole, another pops up on the board. The term is used to describe a situation in which any attempt to deal with a problem is met with another problem, or a recurrence of the original problem.

There is great concern about the issuance of Detention Orders (DOs) by the executive without judicial authority in the PSTA. While the eyes of the critics are fixated on the PSTA, the identical mechanism of detention orders signed by a politically appointed Ministry Secretary appears in the POCA. A concerted effort that leverages UN condemnation, the GSP+ conditions and Constitutional principles may succeed in giving a judge, rather than a political appointee, the authority to approve, modify or reject a request for the DO under the PSTA. But the same Constitutionally problematic provision may get through under POCA. Whack-a-Mole + Flood-the-Zone.

Or take the case of the provisions to extract information from telecom or satellite service providers and platform companies such as Meta in the PSTA (December 2025 draft, section 53). Here, low-level police officers could use Magistrate’s orders obtained through ex-parte and in-camera procedures. Someone must have pointed out these provisions would be counterproductive and inimical to expression of ideas. Commendably, sections 53 and 54 were taken out by the time the PSTA was Gazetted. But they reappear with a few small changes in the POCA Bill. Whack-a-mole.

POCA does not repeal current laws, even partially. For a subset of “serious crimes” described below, the POCA provisions such as those on admissibility of statements may apply in addition to the underlying law (e.g., Penal Code or PSTA).

Overbroad definitions

Early drafts of the Anti-Terrorism Bill and the PSTA had overbroad definitions of terrorism, which has been significantly narrowed and improved in the Gazetted version, but many are still unhappy with it.

What falls within the scope of POCA? Section 3 states: “The provisions of this Act shall apply to the prevention, investigation, prosecution and punishment of offences specified in this Act or First Schedule hereto or any offence punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of either description for four years or more in this Act (referred to as the “serious crime”), where such serious crime is committed by a member of an organised criminal group.”

The first schedule brings in all kinds of statutes, including the Antiquities Ordinance. But the truly dangerous part is the inclusion of “any offence punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of either description for a term of four years or more.” It’s rare nowadays for offences to have the upper limit on imprisonment less than four years.

For example, take the controversial Online Safety Act (OSA) that the NPP Manifesto promised to “amend  . . . by removing restrictions on freedom of expression.” Almost without exception offences created by the OSA carry a maximum term of imprisonment of over four years and would constitute “serious offences” that can enable the executive to slap DOs on suspects and deprive them of liberty in ways contrary to international norms such as Article 9 of the ICCPR. Not all the offences in the old laws enacted by the British suffer from the imprisonment-inflation problem. For example, the highly problematic section 120 of the Penal Code (exciting or attempting to excite disaffection against the state) carries only a two-year maximum. No DOs for those exciting disaffection.

If the Police believe that the actions of any non-randomly formed group of three or more persons constitute serious crimes and therefore fall within the scope of this legislation dire consequences result, such as key provisions of the Evidence Ordinance (for example, section 24 which makes confession made under inducement, threat, or promise) being made inapplicable or relaxed (POCA, Part IV).

Most people may think this is no cause for concern because too many of those who perpetrate organised crimes are not caught or convicted. But the problem is that with the kinds of overbroad and vague definitions used in this bill, all sorts of people who are not engaged in organised crimes may fall within the net and lose protections built into the Evidence Ordinance and related laws. Even if the courts hold in favour of the accused, they would have already been punished by incarceration under administrative DOs.

The PTA was used against organised crime and underworld activities and not against suspected terrorists in 2025, as stated in Parliament by Minister Vijitha Herath. This was described as an interim measure or a workaround. But it can work the other way round too.

Most political activities that may be considered “terroristic” by the Government in power or the security establishment tend to involve more than three persons. The exception would be the psychopaths known as lone-wolf terrorists, who have not appeared in Sri Lanka so far. The offences under the PSTA carry prison terms that would bring them within the scope of POCA. Therefore, POCA is likely to be used on top of the PSTA.

For example, the removal of sections 53 and 54 from the December 2025 draft of the PSTA will actually be just a charade. They are removed from the high-profile PSTA but brought back in by the layering of POCA on top of PSTA. Similarly, the various safeguards regarding admissibility of statements in the current PSTA draft may be nullified by layering POCA above the PSTA.

The effect of this law is not necessarily limited to criminals.

Is this law needed?

Much of what this law seeks to do may be done under the tried and tested provisions of the Penal Code. For example, this bill hinges on the elements “organised criminal group” which “means a structured group of three or more persons, existing for a period of time and acting in concert with the aim of committing one or more serious crimes in order to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit” (s. 66).

That definition, in turn, rests on the definition of a “structured group” which “means a group that is not randomly formed for the immediate commission of a serious crime and that does not need to have formally defined roles for its members, continuity of its membership or a developed structure.” (s. 66)

Why these convoluted definitions within definitions when the concepts of abetment, conspiracy and unlawful assembly in the Penal Code can do the job. But the Minister must explain to us why an entirely new law is needed and why the Penal Code and related legislation cannot do the job.

This law is being enacted as part of a flood-the-zone strategy without any public or stakeholder consultation not because new offences are needed, but because the security establishment and the Government want a workaround for the safeguards in existing law. The flood is not entirely of disconnected, discrete pieces of legislation. In this case, part of it is the organically connected PSTA and POCA.

title: Stranded capital at Colombo Port | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 01:17
-     - 9

There have also been shifts in leadership, with four or five Managing Directors and Project Directors being changed during Phase II, and SLPA has been led by at least four Chairmen since 2021. Each change brings a period of familiarisation, reopens settled questions and weakens accountability, because no single leader has owned the project from design to delivery. Meanwhile, the Board, the Ministry, the Cabinet, procurement committees, the Attorney General, the courts and organised labour each hold  some situational power, and the reality is an expensive, idle terminal. The Sri Lanka Ports Authority, the line Ministry, and other stakeholders must  treat the ECT as a national economic priority. Continued delay costs Sri Lanka foreign exchange it cannot afford to lose. The ECT must deliver the revenue it owes

Few infrastructure assets in South Asia carry as much strategic weight as the East Container Terminal (ECT) at the Port of Colombo. Sitting on one of the busiest transhipment routes between Asia and Europe, it ideally should be a dependable earner of foreign exchange for a country still recovering from the worst economic crisis in its history. Yet, now more than a decade old and owned and developed by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA), it is still not operating as intended despite the substantial public investment already committed.

Economically, the ECT is a case study in how inadequate design, fragmented procurement, and unstable leadership turn productive capital into stranded capital. Every month of further delay adds to a cost that Sri Lanka as a whole must bear due to the consequences of weak decision-making.

A decade of indecision

The first phase of the ECT was completed in mid-2015. For five years, it did not carry the container operations it was built for, denying SLPA the earnings expected from the completed investment.

Compared to other terminals, CICT began construction in December 2011 and operations in July 2013, while CWIT began construction in early 2022 and its first phase of operations in April 2025. As different, their timelines underline the extent of the ECT delay.

Between October 2014 and February 2021, the Cabinet and related bodies took many decisions on the terminal. They awarded a crane contract and rescinded it, endorsed a joint venture and then a public–private partnership before abandoning both, signed a trilateral Memorandum of Cooperation with India and Japan in 2019, and finally decided in February 2021 that SLPA would develop and operate the terminal as a wholly owned facility. Reversals could have been defensible politically, but it was SLPA that carried the idle asset and the interest on the loan. The cost of indecision was not the cost of any single bad choice but the value of the time lost between choices.

Decisions that were SLPA's own

Delays cannot be blamed on Cabinet reversals alone when the authority also made choices. These choices and failures can be salvaged. The SLPA management and its engineers did not prepare a complete, integrated design for the terminal before committing to contracts, one that settled the ground conditions, the yard and gate layout, the operating model, the equipment mix and the systems interfaces together. The terminal was instead designed in pieces as it was built.

In 2021, SLPA set aside both a design consultant and a design-and-build contract, partly because it had no marine soil data for the site, and chose a measure-and-pay contract under which the cost of unforeseen conditions falls on SLPA itself. Soft cohesive soils required additional improvement, and the contract price rose by around 80%.

Equipment was not staggered. The cranes arrived in 2024 and 2025, while the civil works, originally due in January 2025, slipped through three extensions of time (EOTs) to July 2026, with a fourth (EOT 4) requested but not yet granted.

Automation readiness was neglected. A semi-automated terminal needs a stock of critical spare parts, trained maintenance technicians, a proper transfer of technology from the suppliers, and tested operating procedures before its first automated move. There is no evidence that a full census of the spare parts delivered with the 52 cranes has been carried out against the contract schedules, or that the parts have been checked for completeness, condition and storage.

An interface gap was left open for years. The Equipment Control Interface Database (ECI DB), without which the terminal cannot run in semi-automated mode, was first raised in August 2023. The equipment supplier declared it outside its scope, the Attorney General advised arbitration, and more than two and a half years later, the component had still not been procured.

Straddle carriers have been tendered five times since 2021, and four of those processes were cancelled. In the third round, an award that Cabinet had approved was suspended within weeks, reportedly on instruction, and later cancelled after a court challenge by the losing bidder.

People and layouts were left unresolved. The 467 operational and engineering posts identified in 2023 still await approval from the Department of Management Services; there is no Chief Operating Officer, and the proposed operating company awaits the Attorney General's response. The entrance road and building layouts were changed after construction had begun. From these decisions we observe an authority that finds difficult to plan, manage contracts and stick to decisions.

Idle cranes and the weakest link

A container terminal is a tightly integrated system, whose output depends on its weakest component, a logic captured by Michael Kremer's O-ring theory of production. Phase II was split into three packages, civil works, container handling equipment and the Terminal Management System, with no single party accountable for how they fit together.

All 12 ship-to-shore (STS) cranes and forty automated rail-mounted gantry (ARMG) cranes have been delivered. Yet four STS cranes are unutilised, only fourteen ARMGs have been commissioned, and the ARMG fleet in its entirety is reportedly idle. A trial at that stage, operating without straddle carriers, achieved only 7.8 moves per crane per hour. The World Bank's port performance benchmarks suggest over 20.

The ARMGs illustrate the cost of poor sequencing. As the ECT yard was not ready, the cranes were unloaded elsewhere in the port, and some were used there temporarily. They must now be moved and re-erected on their assigned rails, at a cost that was never budgeted and with a risk of damage, misalignment of automation components, and disputes with the supplier over who is responsible for any defects.

Time is of the essence

Delays depreciate what has already been bought, let alone receive revenue. Equipment warranties and defects liability periods usually run from delivery or acceptance, so cranes that arrived in 2024 and 2025 may lose their cover before performing a single commercial move. Software licences, support contracts and IT hardware age in the same way. SLPA may be paying support fees on systems that are not running, may find the installed software nearing the end of its support life before it is used, and will need security updates before connecting an automated terminal to live operations. Cranes standing idle in salt-laden air also deteriorate without lubrication, periodic running and corrosion protection.

The Board must obtain a schedule of every warranty, licence and support expiry, and negotiate extensions while payments to suppliers are still outstanding and SLPA still has some leverage.

The money spent and owed

The two phases are estimated to cost $ 755 million. Of this, $ 550 million had been spent by early 2026. A substantial balance remains to be paid, including for civil works, straddle carriers not yet awarded, equipment, the terminal system and the operation building. The estimates exclude the cost of relocating the ARMGs and any claims not yet decided. It is not clear how the balance will be funded.

Idle capital is never free. At an illustrative 7% cost of capital, the spending already committed to Phase II represents an economic cost of more than $30 million a year before a single revenue-earning move is made.

Contractors and vendors waiting on SLPA

The civil contractor, a joint venture company, is waiting for a decision on EOT 4. Its prolongation claim on earlier extensions was rejected, so it appears to have received time without the associated cost. The contractor lodged a notice of dissatisfaction, often a precursor to FIDIC-based dispute proceedings. Other claims remain uncertified, and physical progress stood at around 80% at that stage. Delayed payments and unresolved claims can add to the slippage. Leaving EOT 4 undecided risks further claims and costs, while postponing the programme needed to complete the remaining works and earn revenue.

There is a real danger that EOT 4 will not be the last. Revetment and dredging works are exposed to turbulent weather. A strong El Niño is predicted too, so the known monsoon risks should already be built in. Marine works should be scheduled for calmer months, with acceleration where needed and close oversight by the Employer and Engineer, so that construction is completed within EOT 4.

The equipment supplier and terminal system vendor are awaiting payments under their contracts. The latter also depends on gate works, OCR portals, the ECI DB, staffing and integration testing. Completing one contract alone cannot make the terminal operational; these activities must be coordinated with the remaining civil works.

Regardless of intentions, contractors will ultimately respond to the credibility of the employer, and undecided claims and unfunded payments do not exactly instill faith in contractors.

The cost of delay

A committee of senior SLPA officers estimates the revenue foregone in 2026 at between  $ 28.2 million and $ 105.6 million, or up to $ 8.8 million a month. In 2027, losses could reach $ 126.7 million if straddle carriers do not arrive. But this does not include actual economic costs of the delay. Only in the better scenario, with carriers from July 2027, does the year turn to a small gain of $ 8.2 million.

These numbers represent the revenue SLPA lost, but do not include the money SLPA is spending while waiting. This includes interest on loans and the costs associated with capital. It also includes preserving, insuring, and securing idle cranes, as well as relocating ARMGs. Furthermore, warranties may expire while licence fees continue. The Engineer’s extended supervision and the contractor’s prolongation costs exacerbate this. Additional money is being spent on repeated re-tendering and on legal and arbitration proceedings. SLPA is also paying staff for an operation that has not yet begun. Nor do they account for the $ 550 million already sunk. Economically, sunk costs should not drive future decisions, but every stagnant year earns that investment nothing and lowers the eventual return entirely. 

The foregone revenue must also be viewed against Colombo’s existing terminal capacity. In 2024, SLPA-run terminals handled 2.41 million TEUs in total, compared with 3.35 million at CICT alone. The figures are not a direct measure of crane productivity, but they underline the importance of bringing ECT’s additional capacity into operation.

Competition is also developing elsewhere in Sri Lanka. Hambantota’s container volumes rose from 53,169 TEUs in 2024 to 428,036 in 2025, and its operator is investing to raise annual handling capacity to 2 million TEUs. Disruptions to shipping routes in the Middle East have made reliable alternatives increasingly important. This does not mean that ECT has already lost business to Hambantota, but prolonged delays may influence where shipping lines choose to call.

The opportunity cost of delay goes beyond revenue foregone in a particular year. Capital tied up in unfinished works cannot be used for improvements elsewhere in the port, while shipping lines plan their services around reliable terminals. Calls lost during the delay may not return even after ECT opens, and the longer-term loss of business is not captured in the committee’s estimates.

The 14 December 2026 date now given for operationalising the terminal should thus be read with care. With straddle carriers not expected before July 2027, it is at best a date for partial operation.

Marking one's own homework: Conflict of interests 

SLPA’s own engineers supervise the construction works and assess delays and contractual claims, including those arising from the Authority’s own instructions and decisions. This creates a clear conflict of interest, as SLPA is effectively assessing the consequences of its own actions. Such an arrangement is inconsistent with global industry best practice, which favours independent third-party engineering oversight and impartial assessment of contractual claims. An independent third-party Engineer should therefore be appointed to supervise the works and assess claims. Similar concerns arise in procurement, where parties with an interest in the straddle carrier award were able to reopen a completed technical evaluation.

There have also been shifts in leadership, with four or five Managing Directors and Project Directors being changed during Phase II, and SLPA has been led by at least four Chairmen since 2021. Each change brings a period of familiarisation, reopens settled questions and weakens accountability, because no single leader has owned the project from design to delivery. Meanwhile, the Board, the Ministry, the Cabinet, procurement committees, the Attorney General, the courts and organised labour each hold a some situational power, and the reality is an expensive, idle terminal. 

What is to be done

The current management deserves credit for convening progress reviews and beginning to take stock, yet there is much to be done. We urge the Board to act hastily on the following:

1.Appoint an independent third-party Engineer to supervise construction and assess claims, supported by port, automation and commissioning specialists reporting to the Board, with a 60 to 90 day mandate to verify the critical path, the cost to complete and the pending claims.

2.Decide EOT 4 now and make it the last extension, on a realistic completion programme allowing for monsoon conditions.

3.Pay what is certified, decide what is claimed, and agree a funded plan for the remaining expenditure.

4.Procure the ECI DB now, while pursuing the dispute with the supplier in parallel.

5.Protect what has been bought through a census of spare parts, a schedule of warranty and licence expiries, and proper preservation of idle equipment.

6.Settle the straddle carrier award on an independent price assessment, and arrange interim operations meanwhile.

7.Approve the cadre, appoint a Chief Operating Officer, enforce the suppliers' training and transfer of technology obligations, and keep one project director in post until completion.

8.Name a single party accountable for systems integration, and report the full cost of delay to the Board every month.

Lessons and an appeal

The ECT experience demonstrates the importance of completing proper site investigations and preparing an integrated design before construction begins. Where different components of a project must coexist, they should either be procured as an integrated system or have a single party responsible for coordinating their interfaces and ensuring compatibility. Civil works, equipment, operating systems and personnel should be planned and coordinated to be readily available. Adequate attention must be given to spare parts, staff training and maintenance requirements, rather than concentrating merely on construction. Cancellations of tenders demonstrates that the lowest procurement price does not equate to the lowest overall cost, particularly when delays postpone revenue generation. Continuity in project leadership and independent scrutiny of major decisions are equally important. Although Cabinet decisions contributed to postponement, the SLPA shares responsibility given the oversights in planning, procurement and decision-making. 

Therefore the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, the line Ministry, and other stakeholders must  treat the ECT as a national economic priority. Continued delay costs Sri Lanka foreign exchange it cannot afford to lose. The ECT must deliver the revenue it owes.

(The author is Head, Department of Economics and Statistics, University of Peradeniya and a former Vice Chairman, Sri Lanka Ports Authority)

title: Sri Lanka throw away a match they should have won | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 03:09
-     - 9

RAWALPINDI: Sri Lanka threw away a golden chance of starting the ODI Tri-Series with a win against host Pakistan when they flung in the towel in a mad 30 minutes or so before the game finished to lose by 37 runs at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium yesterday.

Sri Lanka were cruising to victory at one point, having made a brilliant recovery from 91-4 through a 119-run stand off 107 balls by Pavan Rathnayake (79 off 74 balls, 6 fours, 2 sixes) and Janith Liyanage (60 off 74 balls, 5 fours). They needed 82 off 60 balls and then the equation came down to 58 off 48 balls. With Sri Lanka needing seven an over with five wickets in hand, it was easily gettable, but the shot selections of Rathnayake, Liyanage, and Dasun Shanaka and the way they threw away their wickets in crunch moments, were simply unbearable. The frustration signal by Head Coach Gary Kirsten said it all. Sri Lanka were eventually all out for 268 in the 49th over chasing Pakistan’s total of 305.

Pakistan looked like getting 330 and beyond, but Sri Lanka executed their death bowling pretty well – just 26 runs given away in the final five overs and picking up five wickets in that same period. Salman Agha couldn’t stretch much beyond his well-crafted 107 off 90 balls (10 fours, 1 six), during which he put on stands of 97 off 93 balls and 64 off 46 balls with Hasan Nawaz (37) and Arafat Minhas (18). Agha really paced his innings well and ensured that Sri Lanka never got a grip in the middle overs. But once Agha fell close to the death, the wheels came off for Pakistan as Eshan Malinga in particular showcased his death bowling prowess to end with figures of 4/46.

Player of the Match Agha’s knock was pivotal in helping Pakistan revive a flagging innings after they lost Babar Azam and debutant Saad Baig in quick succession, following a promising third-wicket stand of 74 off 83 balls. On a good batting track, Sri Lanka’s bowlers did well to not let Pakistan’s batters run free, even if they were punished at times for the lack of a genuine fifth bowling option.

title: Future of Sri Lanka Women’s cricket in good space - U19 Coach Ruvin Peiris | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 19 October 2026 03:07
-     - 4

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

With the men’s and women’s teams going through lean periods in their cricket, the women’s Under-19 cricketers’ victory in the Pakistan Women’s Under-19 T20 Tri-Series came as a soothing balm to the country’s cricketing fraternity, who have been clamouring for success over the years.

The Sri Lanka U19 women cricketers lost only their first match of the Tri-Series, but after that, they were unstoppable, going on to beat Bangladesh by four runs in a thrilling final to lift the cup.

“The momentum and credit for the win should go to the players,” said Sri Lanka U19 Women’s Head Coach Ruvin Peiris. “Through sheer hard work, they have got this result. They are the ones who took decisions in the middle and handled the situations, so all credit to them. The win has boosted their confidence levels very high. They understand that if they put in the hard yards, they can beat any side.”

“We didn’t underestimate the Bangladesh team, because from the very inception of the tournament, we realised that they were a good side. They were a side that had beaten us on previous occasions. We were prepared to face a situation like this in the final,” added Peiris. “The final was a special game. I don’t think the players were under any pressure but in that game, we made the most mistakes, especially in our fielding. We were the best fielding side in the tournament but in the final, we made a lot of mistakes with several catches dropped. They are 16, 17-year-old girls and I believe these mistakes are part of the game. Because of the intensity, there is always room to make mistakes.”

The Tri-Series Peiris said was part of their preparations for the Under-19 Women’s T20 World Cup in January 2027 in Bangladesh and Nepal.

“We are playing these matches with an eye on the 2027 U19 Women’s T20 World Cup. For this entire year, we have planned to prepare for it. This process is really good because all these players will be available for selection for the World Cup,” said Peiris.

Sri Lanka have the Under-19 T20 Asia Cup in early December at a venue yet to be selected, and after that, it will be the Under-19 T20 World Cup. But, in between, Peiris said that Sri Lanka Cricket was looking to slot in another series so that the players will have more international match exposure behind them.

Peiris said the experience they gained from playing in India served them well in the Pakistan Women’s Under-19 T20 Tri-Series. It was Peiris’ first assignment as Head Coach of the Under-19 Women’s team. 

Sri Lanka had begun their preparations for the U19 World Cup with a win in the Under-19 Tri-Series in Australia that also involved England. 

“We didn’t have much success on that tour to India, losing both the ODIs and T20Is by 3-0 margins. But the experience we gained from playing against such a strong side helped us win this Tri-Series,” said Peiris. “We corrected most of our shortcomings. From that series, we realised where our cricket stood and that we needed to put in more effort. From there onwards, the girls improved their individual skills.”

“If you take India, they are a strong side, they are in a different sphere. It was a good experience for us to play India before the World Cup. From that experience, we are developing our cricket and trying to uplift it. Indian cricketers are very much matured because they play about 100 domestic matches in different formats during the year, whereas our girls hardly play even 25.
